subtype: Approach: ignoring warning signs of burnout [Pitfall]
passage: “Sonali, sit down. I'll tell you something I never told your mother. I'm Chaitanya, your uncle. When I was sixteen I studied for the entrance test from five till midnight. The headaches started in the second month. I turned short-tempered and snapped at my sister for nothing. Every time the coaching bell rang, my stomach turned over with dread. I told myself only weak boys complain, so I pushed on. In exam week I sat down at the desk and my mind went blank. Not tired: empty. I read the same question eleven times. I lost the seat I'd worked a year for. What I regret isn't the seat. It's that for four months I brushed off every sign my own body gave me.”

qa.q: How many times did Chaitanya read the same question in exam week?
What did Chaitanya feel each time the coaching bell rang?
qa.a: Dread: his stomach turned over, and he brushed it off as weakness.

qa.q: At what point in the story could a different choice have changed things?
qa.a: When the headaches began in the second month, telling someone or easing the schedule then might have prevented the collapse, instead of telling himself only weak boys complain.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya's sister have experienced those months?
qa.a: She was snapped at for no reason by a brother who seemed to have lost his patience, and may have felt hurt or worried without knowing why.

grounding: An elder recalls dismissing headaches, irritability and dread as weakness, pushing on and ending in a blank exam week.
